q: how to handle memory leaks in c++
how to avoid memory leaks in c++
how to detect memory leaks in c++
a: C++ memory management follows RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): resources are tied to object lifetimes and released in destructors. Modern C++ avoids raw `new`/`delete` in favor of smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`) and STL containers. A memory leak occurs when dynamically allocated memory is never deleted. Use RAII wrappers, avoid manual resource management, and use tools like Valgrind, AddressSanitizer (ASan), or `std::unique_ptr` to prevent leaks. Follow the Rule of Five for classes managing raw resources.

q: how to use vectors in c++
how to iterate over vector in c++
a: `std::vector` is a dynamic array that grows automatically. Access elements with `[]` (no bounds check) or `.at()` (throws `std::out_of_range`). Add elements with `push_back` or `emplace_back` (constructs in-place). Use `reserve()` to pre-allocate capacity for performance. Iteration options: index loop, range-based for, iterators, or algorithms. `size()` returns element count, `capacity()` returns allocated storage. `shrink_to_fit()` reduces capacity to fit size.

q: how to use unique_ptr in c++
how to manage memory in c++ with smart pointers
a: Smart pointers in `<memory>` automate memory management. `std::unique_ptr` is exclusive ownership (non-copyable, movable) — default for single-owner resources. `std::shared_ptr` uses reference counting for shared ownership; use `std::make_shared` for efficiency. `std::weak_ptr` breaks circular references by holding a non-owning reference to a `shared_ptr`. Always use `std::make_unique` and `std::make_shared` instead of `new` for exception safety and performance. Custom deleters are supported.

q: how to use classes in c++
c++ access specifiers public private protected
a: C++ classes encapsulate data and behavior. Use access specifiers: `public` (accessible anywhere), `protected` (accessible in class and derived), `private` (accessible only in class). Constructors initialize members; use the member initializer list for efficiency. Destructors clean up resources. Virtual functions enable polymorphism with `override` keyword (C++11+) for safety. Follow the Rule of Three/Five for resource-managing classes. Use `= default` and `= delete` for special member functions.

q: how to use stl algorithms in c++
how to use lambda with stl algorithms c++
a: The STL algorithms library (`<algorithm>`, `<numeric>`) provides generic functions operating on ranges via iterators. Key categories: sorting (`sort`, `stable_sort`, `partial_sort`), searching (`find`, `binary_search`, `lower_bound`), modifying (`copy`, `transform`, `replace`, `fill`), and numeric (`accumulate`, `inner_product`, `partial_sum`). Most algorithms accept callables (function pointers, lambdas, `std::function`). Lambdas are preferred for short predicates. Use `constexpr` and ranges (C++20) for modern code.

q: how to use pointers in c++
how to use pointers and references in c++
a: Pointers store memory addresses. Declare with `T* ptr`. Get an address with `&` (address-of), access value with `*` (dereference). Always initialize pointers to `nullptr` (C++11) rather than `NULL` or `0`. Use references (`T&`) when you don't need reseating or null state — they're safer. Pointer arithmetic moves by `sizeof(T)` increments. Smart pointers (`unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`) should replace raw owning pointers. Raw pointers are only for non-owning observation.
